Title: Knee-xRAI: An Explainable AI Framework for Automatic Kellgren-Lawrence Grading of Knee Osteoarthritis

Knee-xRAI: An Explainable AI Framework for
Automatic Kellgren–Lawrence Grading of Knee
Osteoarthritis
Azmul A. Irfan1⋆, Nur Ahmad Khatim2, Alfan Alfian Irfan3, Achmad Zaki1, Erike A. Suwarsono1,
and Mansur M. Arief4
Abstract—Radiographic grading of knee osteoarthritis (KOA)
with the Kellgren–Lawrence (KL) system is limited by inter-
reader variability and by the opacity of current deep learning
approaches, which predict KL grades directly from images without
decomposing the structural features that define disease severity.
We present Knee-xRAI, a modular framework that independently
quantifies the three cardinal radiographic features of KOA (joint
space narrowing, osteophytes, and subchondral sclerosis) and
integrates them into an explainable KL grade classification. The
pipeline combines U-Net++ segmentation for contour-based JSN
measurement, an SE-ResNet-50 multi-task network for per-site
osteophyte grading on an OARSI-aligned ordinal scale, and a
hybrid texture-CNN classifier for binary sclerosis quantification.
The resulting 50-dimensional structured feature vector feeds two
complementary classification paths. An XGBoost path supports
SHAP-based, feature-based attribution. A ConvNeXt hybrid path
combines the structured vector with a full-image encoder for better
predictive performance. Evaluated on 8,260 knee radiographs
from a publicly available OAI-derived dataset, the JSN module
achieved a Dice coefficient of 0.8909 and an mJSW intraclass
correlation of 0.8674 against manual annotations. The ConvNeXt
hybrid path reached a test quadratic weighted kappa (QWK)
of 0.8436 and AUC of 0.9017, while the transparent XGBoost
path achieved a test QWK of 0.6294 with full feature-level audit
capability. Ablation analysis confirmed JSN as the dominant
tabular predictor (QWK = 0.6103 alone), with osteophyte features
providing a consistent incremental gain (∆QWK = +0.0183)
and sclerosis features contributing marginally on the current
annotation scale. A complementary inference-time ablation of Path
B confirmed that the structured pathway contributes materially
beyond the image encoder, with QWK drops of 0.098 under
feature zeroing and 0.284 under feature–image permutation. To
our knowledge, Knee-xRAI is the first published framework to
explicitly quantify all three KL-defining radiographic features
within a single auditable pipeline.
Index Terms—Knee osteoarthritis, Kellgren–Lawrence grading,
explainable artificial intelligence, joint space narrowing, osteo-
phytes, subchondral sclerosis, deep learning.

I. INTRODUCTION
K
NEE osteoarthritis (KOA) affects approximately 654
million adults aged 40 years and older [1] and is a leading
cause of lower-limb disability worldwide [2]. The burden is
particularly acute in low- and middle-income health systems.
In Indonesia, a population of 26.8 million adults 60 years of
age or older [3] is served by only 1.2 radiologists per 100,000
people [4]. In such settings, radiographic interpretation is
routinely delegated to non-subspecialist clinicians. Interpretable
diagnostic support, whose reasoning can be audited without
the expertise of a radiologist, is therefore a practical rather
than theoretical requirement, paralleling recent AI-driven knee
radiograph analysis efforts in healthcare settings [5].
Radiographic severity follows the Kellgren–Lawrence (KL)
score, a five-grade ordinal system (0 to 4) defined by three
cardinal findings: JSN, osteophyte formation, and subchondral
sclerosis [6]. Inter-reader variability, compounded by multiple
divergent KL descriptions in the literature [7], carries direct
clinical consequences. A single-grade disagreement can redirect
a patient from conservative physiotherapy to intra-articular
corticosteroid injection, or alter eligibility for orthopaedic
referral [8].
Automated methods have emerged to address this shortfall.
Deep learning approaches have reached QWK values of up
to 0.83 and multiclass accuracies greater than 66% [9], yet
they typically compress three distinct pathological features
into a single opaque prediction justified by post-hoc saliency
maps that produce no auditable artifact tied to a named clinical
finding [10]. Partial advances exist. MediAI-OA [11] quantifies
the JSN and osteophyte burden but omits sclerosis entirely,
diverging from radiological best practice. To our knowledge, no
published framework quantifies all three KL-defining features
concurrently within a single auditable grade.
This study addresses this gap with Knee-xRAI, an inter-
pretable framework that explicitly quantifies the three principal
structural components of KOA from plain radiographs and uses
them to support the ordinal KL classification. We hypothesize
that a concept-based, feature-decomposed design can deliver KL
classification performance competitive with end-to-end deep
learning models while substantially improving interpretability
and clinical usability, and that the resulting feature-level outputs
can serve as an audit surface for clinician readers in resource-
constrained settings.

II. RELATED WORK
A. End-to-End KL Grade Classification
Most previous AI approaches predict the KL grade directly
from the radiograph. Chen et al. [12] combined YOLOv2
detection with a CNN classifier, achieving 69.7% five-class
accuracy, while Pi et al. [13] demonstrated that CNN ensembles
improve robustness. More recently, Ullah and Kim [15]
integrated a ViT-L16 backbone with CORAL ordinal regression
and CLIP-based visual–language alignment, yielding state-
of-the-art macro F1 on the OAI dataset. Hierarchical CNN
ensembles [16] further illustrate this end-to-end paradigm. None
of these methods explicitly identifies the structural findings that
support the predicted grade, a limitation that largely reflects
the cost and scarcity of per-feature annotations and constrains
adoption in clinical workflows where transparency is essential.
B. Feature-Specific Quantification
For JSN, Guo et al. [17] applied TransUNet for joint-
space segmentation, achieving Dice = 0.889 and ICC =
0.927, and subsequently combined JSW values with XGBoost
for 72-month longitudinal prediction; MediAI-OA [11] nor-
malizes mJSW to a continuous JSN rate, closely aligned
with the approach adopted here. For osteophytes, Tiulpin
and Saarakkala [9] trained SE-ResNet-50 and SE-ResNeXt-50
ensembles to simultaneously predict KL grades and six OARSI
feature grades [18], achieving per-site osteophyte kappas of
0.79–0.94 on 11,743 knees, demonstrating the feasibility of
per-site ordinal grading with attention-augmented CNNs. For
subchondral sclerosis, Kim et al. [14] trained EfficientNet-B0
for three-level sclerosis classification on 4,019 knee radiographs,
achieving AUC = 0.952, while Bayramoglu et al. [19] showed
that LBP with an adaptive subchondral ROI strategy achieved
AUC = 0.840, providing methodological justification for the
hybrid texture–CNN design adopted in the sclerosis module.
C. Explainability in KOA Diagnosis
Grad-CAM [20] is the most widely used post-hoc visual-
ization technique in medical imaging and has been applied to
KOA by Karim et al. [21]. Weber et al. [10] documented that
post-hoc heatmaps may not faithfully represent the features
a model relies upon, a concern they term the interpretation
gap. Broader critiques of post-hoc XAI have called for a
paradigm shift toward mechanistically transparent systems [22].
VL-OrdinalFormer [15] moves toward concept-based modeling

D. Research Gap
As Table I summarizes, existing KOA models remain divided
between end-to-end classifiers with strong performance but
without structural decomposition and feature-specific stud-
ies that have investigated JSN, osteophytes, and sclerosis
predominantly in isolation. Knee-xRAI addresses this gap
through a four-stage pipeline (JSN segmentation, osteophyte
ROI grading, sclerosis texture classification, and dual-path
feature aggregation) detailed in the following section.
III. METHODS
A. Dataset, Preprocessing, and Evaluation Protocol
All experiments used the publicly available Knee Osteo-
arthritis Severity Grading Dataset [12], [23], which comprises
8,260 grayscale posteroanterior knee radiographs at 224 × 224
pixels, partitioned 70:10:20 into training (n=5,778), validation
(n=826), and test (n=1,656) sets. The grade distribution is
markedly imbalanced across all splits, with KL0 dominant
(39.4%, n=3,253) and KL4 rare (3.0%, n=251). Feature-
level annotations were compiled on subsets of 400–500
images each. These comprised polyline articular contours for
JSN segmentation, OARSI ordinal grades per-site (0–3) at

The images were preprocessed with CLAHE (clip limit
3.0, tile grid 8 × 8 px), clipping of the 5th–99th percentile
intensity, normalization to [0, 1], and ImageNet standardization
(µ=0.485, σ=0.229). Training-time augmentation included
random rotation (±10◦), horizontal flip (p=0.5), brightness
and contrast jitter (±15%), and affine scaling within [0.9, 1.1].
We addressed class imbalance through batch sampling with
inverse-frequency and an ordinal soft-label cross-entropy loss
with Gaussian smoothing (σ=0.5). Two module-specific prepro-
cessing distinctions apply. For the osteophyte stage, full-image
CLAHE precedes 140 × 140 patch extraction but is not re-
applied to extracted ROIs, to avoid double enhancement. For
the sclerosis stage, CLAHE is deliberately withheld because
the hybrid classifier relies on handcrafted texture descriptors
(GLCM statistics, fractal dimension) that are sensitive to the
natural subchondral intensity distribution.
Evaluation metrics were selected per module. JSN segmen-
tation used the Dice coefficient and HD95, with ICC against
manual mJSW as the primary measurement-fidelity criterion.
Osteophyte grading was performed with quadratic-weighted
kappa per-site (κ) and AUC, and sclerosis classification used
macro F1, balanced accuracy, and AUC. The KL prediction was
evaluated primarily by QWK, with accuracy, macro F1, and
macro AUC as secondary metrics. Two complementary ablation
studies quantified per-family contributions under Path A and
the marginal contribution of the structured pathway under Path
B. Where reported, 95% confidence intervals were obtained
by percentile bootstrap with 1,000 resamples. All models were
implemented in PyTorch 2.0 with PyTorch Lightning on a
single NVIDIA RTX 4090.
B. Knee-xRAI Framework
Knee-xRAI decomposes KL grading into four sequential
stages (Fig. 1).
1) Stage 1: JSN Segmentation and Quantification:
We trained a U-Net++ [24] with an ImageNet-pretrained
EfficientNet-B4 encoder [25] to produce three-class masks

(lr = 1×10−4) and cosine annealing. Checkpoint selection
used minimum mJSW MAE rather than peak Dice to prioritize
measurement fidelity. For each compartment c ∈{med, lat},
we sampled 16 equidistant femoral landmark points along the
mediolateral axis with endpoint trimming to suppress false
minima. The minimum joint space width is defined as

2) Stage 2: Osteophyte ROI Extraction and Ordinal Grading:
Site patches of 140 × 140 pixels at four anatomical locations
(medial and lateral femur, medial and lateral tibia) were located
through a three-tier cascade: Stage-1 segmentation landmarks
as the primary source, a heuristic anatomical estimator as
fallback where the mask was absent or too small, and fixed
geometric crops as a last resort. Ordinal grading was performed
by a multi-task SE-ResNet-50 [26] with four site-specific MLP
heads trained using ordinal cross-entropy loss. Site-specific fine-
tuning was applied to the lateral femur and medial tibia based
on validation performance, a choice we revisit in the Discussion.
The osteophyte sub-vector is 10-dimensional, encoding four
site-specific grades, total burden, maximum site grade, and
four composite scores.
3) Stage 3: Sclerosis ROI Extraction and Binary Classifi-
cation: Subchondral ROIs were defined as the bone region
immediately inferior to the tibial plateau from the Stage-1
mask, following the anatomy-guided strategy of Bayramoglu
et al. [19]. A hybrid classifier combined handcrafted tex-
ture features (multi-scale LBP histograms at radii 1, 2, 3;
GLCM statistics; fractal dimension; per-compartment intensity
statistics) with a parallel EfficientNet-B0 image branch, fused
through a two-layer MLP. A binary formulation (none vs.
present) was adopted after the three-class scheme proved
unstable under the available mild-sclerosis annotation volume.
The decision threshold was optimized on the validation set at
τ=0.4227 to maximize macro F1. The sclerosis sub-vector is
18-dimensional.
4) Stage 4: Feature Aggregation and KL Classification:
The three sub-vectors are concatenated and z-score normalized
into a 50-dimensional structured feature vector,

which feeds two complementary classification paths. Path
A (XGBoost) trains a gradient-boosted classifier [27] (300
estimators, depth 6, lr =0.05, L1/L2 regularisation) with 5-fold
stratified cross-validation, with SHAP [28] attribution providing
fully auditable feature-level explanations. Path B (ConvNeXt
Hybrid) concatenates a ConvNeXt-Small [29] image encoding
(768-dim) with an MLP-projected feature vector (256-dim),
fused through a fusion MLP for five-class ordinal prediction
with soft-label cross-entropy (σ=0.5). A Gradio interface
exposes three explainability layers: feature-level outputs (mJSW,
JSN rates, per-site OARSI grades, texture statistics), spatial
overlays from directly measured features rather than post-hoc
gradients, and a path toggle with updated class probabilities.
The full pipeline processes a single radiograph in under 10
seconds.
IV. EXPERIMENTS AND RESULTS
A. JSN Segmentation and Measurement Performance
We evaluated U-Net++ performance on the 60-image an-
notated evaluation subset. The manual-teacher checkpoint
achieved Dice = 0.8904 and HD95 = 1.4734 px, comparable
to the TransUNet benchmark of Guo et al. [17] (Dice = 0.889),
with ICC = 0.8699 indicating good-to-excellent reproducibility
of mJSW (ICC ≥0.75 per Koo and Li [30]). The self-
trained variant achieved a similar Dice (0.8894) but incurred a
higher MAE (1.7217 vs. 1.7020 px) and a lower ICC (0.8645
vs. 0.8699). Because downstream feature quality depends on
measurement fidelity rather than segmentation overlap alone,
we selected the manual-teacher checkpoint, yielding a deployed
result of Dice = 0.8909, HD95 = 1.4964 px, MAE = 1.7041 px,
and ICC = 0.8674. Qualitative JSN visualizations are shown
in Fig. 2.
B. Osteophyte Grading Performance
The grading performance was heterogeneous across the four
anatomical sites (Table II). The medial femur achieved the
strongest held-out test kappa (κ=0.5828, AUC = 0.6872),
followed by the medial tibia (κ=0.4706, AUC = 0.7105).
The lateral femur exhibited a substantial validation-to-test
gap, with a validation kappa of 0.6660 falling to 0.1048
in the test set. This reflects the limited per-site annotation
volume combined with the inherent ambiguity of lateral femoral
osteophytes in two-dimensional AP projections. The pseudo-
label expansion amplified the teacher bias rather than resolving
the gap (expanded mean test κ=0.3791 vs. 0.3812 for the
manual-teacher framework). We therefore retained the manual-
teacher framework for all downstream feature extraction, though
the lateral femur standalone output should be interpreted with
caution.

C. Subchondral Sclerosis Classification
Threshold optimization on the validation set identified
τ=0.4227 as the value maximizing macro F1. On the annotated
subset (n=150 per split), the classifier reached a validation
macro F1 of 0.6212 [95% CI 0.5390, 0.6866] and AUC of
0.6709 [0.5867, 0.7552], with test macro F1 = 0.5785 [0.4977,
0.6582] and AUC = 0.6114 [0.5245, 0.7003]; accuracy and
balanced accuracy tracked these values within 0.01 on both
splits. Comparison against five classical texture-based baselines
confirmed that the hybrid classifier was competitive. Extra
Trees, the strongest baseline, reached a test macro F1 of 0.5696
and AUC of 0.6204. Representative ROI outputs are shown in
Fig. 3. As the test-set AUC CI lower bound approaches 0.52,
we return to this module’s modest absolute performance in the
Discussion.
D. KL Grade Classification
Path A (XGBoost) achieved a test QWK of 0.6294 (5-
fold CV QWK 0.6467 ± 0.0109), accuracy 0.5399, macro
F1 0.5238, and AUC 0.8046, while Path B (ConvNeXt hybrid)
substantially outperformed with a test QWK of 0.8436, accuracy
0.6636, macro F1 0.6693, and AUC 0.9017 (Table III). Per-class
analysis (Table IV) identified KL grade 1 as the most difficult
category for both paths, with F1 scores of 0.0817 and 0.3798,
respectively, consistent with the inherent diagnostic ambiguity
of doubtful disease characterised by possible osteophytes
without definite JSN. Path B’s largest absolute gains over Path
A occurred at KL2 (∆=+0.2179) and KL0 (∆=+0.1400),
the two grades for which fine-grained visual context most
supplements the handcrafted feature representation.
1) Path A Feature Ablation: Table V reports six feature-
subset configurations evaluated on the held-out test set under
Path A. JSN features alone were the strongest single-family
predictor (QWK = 0.6103), substantially above osteophyte-
only (0.4078) and sclerosis-only (0.2396) subsets. Adding
osteophyte features produced a consistent incremental gain
(∆QWK=+0.0183, from 0.6103 to 0.6286), confirming that
per-site osteophyte burden carries independent predictive
information beyond the joint space profile. Including sclerosis
in the full tri-feature vector yielded only marginal additional
improvement (∆QWK=+0.0008), reflecting the constrained
signal available from the current binary representation. Fig. 4
shows the ablation QWK chart alongside the SHAP beeswarm
plot.

structured vector’s marginal contribution, we applied inference-
time zeroing and permutation to the trained ConvNeXt hybrid
without retraining (Table VI). Zeroing all 50 dimensions drops

V. DISCUSSION
A. Key Findings and Clinical Interpretation
Because KL grades 2–4 are operationally defined by the
presence and severity of JSN [6], the joint-space profile
emerges as the most decisive single predictor, with per-
site osteophyte features encoding complementary information
not fully captured by the JSW profile alone. The lateral
femur validation-to-test gap reflects limited annotation volume
compounded by the inherent two-dimensional ambiguity of
lateral femoral osteophytes in AP projections. The sclerosis
performance gap relative to Kim et al. [14] (AUC 0.611 vs.
0.952) is attributable to structural differences in experimental
design rather than an absence of radiographic signal, and at its
present annotation scale the sclerosis module serves primarily
as a structural completeness component that closes the three-
feature claim and enables feature-level reporting.
B. Transparency–Performance Trade-off
The QWK gap between Path A and Path B quantifies the cost
of mechanistic transparency, yet the inference-time ablation
establishes that the structured pathway is not redundant with
the image encoder. The three-fold difference between zeroing
and permutation confirms feature–image alignment rather than
static-covariate use, with the contribution concentrated in the
JSN sub-vector. Although osteophyte and sclerosis dimensions
add little to Path B beyond what ConvNeXt recovers from the
image, both remain indispensable for Path A’s audit surface
through SHAP-based attribution [28] to named radiographic
concepts of direct value in radiologist-shortage settings.
C. Limitations
The 224×224 px PNG format lacks calibrated DICOM pixel
spacing, so mJSW values are pixel-based and millimetre conver-
sion requires a user-supplied scale factor. Feature-level annota-
tion sets are small (400–500 images per module), constraining
generalisation most acutely at the lateral femur site, where the
sclerosis test AUC CI lower bound approaches chance. Inter-
annotator reliability was not formally quantified; annotations
were expert-reviewed by two orthopaedic practitioners but lack
a kappa agreement score. Finally, no external validation has
been conducted, and pipeline robustness to institutional and
acquisition variability, including the Indonesian-deployment
contexts motivating this work, remains to be established.
VI. CONCLUSION
Knee-xRAI demonstrates that interpretability in AI-assisted
KOA grading need not depend on post-hoc saliency attribution
but can instead be built into the diagnostic pipeline through
explicit, independently quantified structural features from each
step of the KL grading process. By decomposing the KL grade
into its three cardinal radiographic constituents and exposing
each as a measurable, named clinical finding, the framework
produces a grade that is a deterministic function of auditable
evidence rather than an opaque model output. The primary
contribution is not incremental accuracy improvement over
end-to-end models but the demonstration that a clinically
structured, feature-decomposed pipeline can approach deep
learning classification performance while producing the kind of
transparent reasoning that clinicians in resource-constrained
settings can inspect, question, and trust.

Abstract: Radiographic grading of knee osteoarthritis (KOA) with the Kellgren–Lawrence (KL) system is limited by inter- reader variability and by the opacity of current deep learning approaches, which predict KL grades directly from images without decomposing the structural features that define disease severity. We present Knee-xRAI, a modular framework that independently quantifies the three cardinal radiographic features of KOA (joint space narrowing, osteophytes, and subchondral sclerosis) and integrates them into an explainable KL grade classification. The pipeline combines U-Net++ segmentation for contour-based JSN measurement, an SE-ResNet-50 multi-task network for per-site osteophyte grading on an OARSI-aligned ordinal scale, and a hybrid texture-CNN classifier for binary sclerosis quantification. The resulting 50-dimensional structured feature vector feeds two complementary classification paths. An XGBoost path supports SHAP-based, feature-based attribution. A ConvNeXt hybrid path combines the structured vector with a full-image encoder for better predictive performance. Evaluated on 8,260 knee radiographs from a publicly available OAI-derived dataset, the JSN module achieved a Dice coefficient of 0.8909 and an mJSW intraclass correlation of 0.8674 against manual annotations. The ConvNeXt hybrid path reached a test quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) of 0.8436 and AUC of 0.9017, while the transparent XGBoost path achieved a test QWK of 0.6294 with full feature-level audit capability. Ablation analysis confirmed JSN as the dominant tabular predictor (QWK = 0.6103 alone), with osteophyte features providing a consistent incremental gain (∆QWK = +0.0183) and sclerosis features contributing marginally on the current annotation scale. A complementary inference-time ablation of Path B confirmed that the structured pathway contributes materially beyond the image encoder, with QWK drops of 0.098 under feature zeroing and 0.284 under feature–image permutation. To our knowledge, Knee-xRAI is the first published framework to explicitly quantify all three KL-defining radiographic features within a single auditable pipeline.
